SET CONTRACT (the engine depends on every line of it)
FORMAT
- One SVG per set, viewBox="0 0 2400 1350". The visible frame is the centred 1920 x 1080 area; mark it with

  the whole 2400 x 1350 canvas (overscan for camera pushes and pans); mid and near may stop at the frame edge.
- Three top-level groups in this order: <g id="far">, <g id="mid">, <g id="near">. Inside them, one named group per
  object (lowercase snake_case: table, chair_3, wall_screen, window_2). Draw the walls and the floor complete behind
  the furniture, so nothing has a hole when the layers slide apart.
- Light and surface effects go in classed groups inside each depth group: class="lm-shadow" (cast and contact
  shadows), class="lm-light" (light patches), class="lm-atmos" (haze, light shafts), class="lm-texture" (texture
  marks), class="lm-outline" (strokes, only if the style uses outlines), class="lm-hi" (highlight edges),
  class="lm-glow" (glow, only if the style uses it). Base shapes stay outside these groups.
- No <text>, no letters or numbers anywhere, no <image>, no filters, no masks, no clip paths, no external references.
  Gradients only where the style block allows them: two stops, palette colours only.
- Up to 700 KB per file; coordinates as integers or one decimal.
- Every position in the brief below (percent of height, thirds, left and right) refers to the visible 1920 x 1080
  frame, not the canvas.
- A mid or near object cropped by a frame edge continues at least 120 px into the overscan, so a camera move never
  shows its cut edge.

LIGHTS AND LIT THINGS (which palette tones draw them)
- A lit screen face: paper hi (the slot rect sits on it). A screen that is off: screen tones.
- Small lights (an exit sign, an LED, a card reader, a lift indicator): plant hi for green, accent hi for red, with
  lm-glow around them only if the style uses glow.
- A lamp's or a screen's spill on nearby surfaces: light at 0.3 to 0.6 fill-opacity in lm-light (a cool screen spill:
  glass base at 0.1 to 0.2).
- Night window glass: sky deep, with shadow over it at about 0.6 fill-opacity in lm-shadow; distant city lights as
  small light-coloured dots.
- A light or shadow shape lies only on the surface it lands on. Where an object of the same layer stands on that
  surface (a chair on a sunlit floor, a cup in a pane pattern on a table), the shape stops at the object's outline and
  never paints across it; light that falls on the object itself is drawn on the object's own shapes. A shadow or light
  shape laid over a chair makes the chair look like glass (the office sets of 2026-10-12).

STYLE: ISOMETRIC (for systems, processes and whole places seen from above; how a floor or a workflow is laid out)
- True isometric on a 2:1 grid (30 degree axes), no perspective, no vanishing points; one base grid unit of 64 px so every prop sits on whole units.
- Rooms are cutaways: the floor and two back walls, the two front walls cut at a low height (about 1/4 of the wall) so the inside is visible; the cut edge is shown as a clean band in the deep shade.
- Three tones per volume: top face highlight (lit), left face base, right face shade; an optional 1.5 px outline in the deep tone of each material (not black).
- Scale for small figures: people are 80 to 160 px tall, so furniture is drawn to that scale and kept simple but exact.
- Show material thickness: walls have a visible thickness band at the cut, windows have reveals, tables have edges; one shadow type and one shadow angle throughout; no screen or multiply effects.
- Light: Fixed light from top left: top faces lightest, right faces darkest; cast shadows as flat parallelograms to the right on the floor at 0.2 opacity.
- Texture: None; floor tiles or planks as a grid of thin lines in the floor shade.
- Depth: Not layered by distance: deliver the room as one isometric group plus a separate group per piece of furniture (so the engine can sort and animate them).

THE WORLD: METAPHOR WORLDS
A fictional fishing harbour town of about 600 people on a granite headland on a cold North Atlantic coast, in late May, when icebergs drift south past the coast. The town sits around a small sheltered harbour that opens to the east; a white lighthouse stands on the headland south of the harbour mouth, with its keeper's house and a walled kitchen garden in the lee of the tower; behind the town a footpath climbs a bare hill to a summit cairn; across the narrow inlet north of the town a new concrete road bridge is being built from both banks. Every set is a spot in this one place, so the same lighthouse, the same granite and the same sea recur. No real town is drawn.
Architecture:

- the harbour: a straight quay of squared granite blocks with a concrete capping, black cast-iron bollards about 5 m apart and 0.5 m back from the edge, vertical timber fenders on the quay face, a steel ladder recessed into the wall; a curved rubble breakwater of big granite blocks across the south side of the harbour mouth, with a short white light tower with a red lantern on its head, and a small green light on a white post at the quay's end
- single-storey fishing stores along the quay: timber sheds with pitched roofs of dark grey corrugated sheet, wide double doors, weathered silver-grey boards
- the lighthouse: a round tapering tower of white-painted masonry about 18 m tall on the headland's highest rock, a black-painted iron gallery with railings, a glazed lantern with diagonal glazing bars and a red-painted domed roof with a ball vent; inside, below the lantern, a round watch room holds the weight-driven clockwork that still turns the lens; the station is kept as a working heritage light, wound by hand by a part-time keeper
- the land: bare grey-pink granite in rounded outcrops and cliffs, low wind-shaped spruce in the hollows, crowberry and grass heath, small dark ponds; no tall trees
- the new bridge: a concrete box-girder road bridge built by the balanced cantilever method, two slim piers in the inlet, each carrying a deck that grows outward both ways in 5 m segments, with yellow form travellers at the tips of the growing deck and a tower crane beside each pier
Materials: grey-pink granite, painted clapboard (muted ochre, oxblood, slate blue, off-white), silver-grey weathered timber, black cast iron and painted steel, white-painted masonry, fresh pale-grey concrete, rope and netting, a deep blue-green sea and white-and-pale-blue ice; signal red and orange only on things that carry them in life (the lantern roof, the breakwater light, lifebuoys, fishing floats, a rescue boat's collar), and warning yellow only on the bridge's construction plant (the cranes, the form travellers). THE SET TO DRAW: iceberg: a single iceberg on the open sea off the headland, shown as a cutaway at the waterline: the white part above the sea and the far larger blue part below it, drawn to true proportions (shots it serves: wide; used for hidden risk and hidden cost, what is visible versus what is not (culture, technical debt, unconscious bias, root causes), early warning, why a small sign matters)
Plan (draw from it; positions in the frame below come from this camera):
- ABSTRACT (a cutaway, not a camera view): the water below the waterline is drawn clear, as a cross-section that no camera could see, so this composition is set directly in frame terms and was not plan-checked. Everything ABOVE the waterline is a normal view from a boat at sea level; everything BELOW is a flat section through the berg's middle.
- Proportions are real and fixed at one scale for the whole picture: 1 m = 5.5 px, both across and down.
- The berg: a medium iceberg of glacier ice, about 30 m above the water and 80 m long at the waterline. Its keel reaches about 120 m below the water (a draft about four times its height, between the measured averages for domed and blocky bergs) and is wider than the visible part, up to about 150 m across, so the area under the waterline is about nine times the area above it (ice floats with about nine tenths of its volume under water).
- The sea here is about 200 m deep: the seabed is below the frame and is not drawn.
- For scale: a small inshore fishing boat (11 m long) on the surface at the left, well clear of the berg.
Camera: Two views joined at the waterline. Above it: a camera at sea level looking straight out to sea, so the horizon is the waterline itself, a dead level line at y 300 (28 percent) across the frame. Below it: a flat, square-on cross-section with no perspective. No tilt, no vanishing points below the water; the scale is 5.5 px per metre throughout.
Composition: The waterline is a level line at y 300 across the whole canvas. Above it, the berg's visible part is the bright shape right of centre: it meets the water from x 920 to x 1360 (80 m), rises in a rounded shoulder on the left and a steep cliff on the right to its top at x 1190, y 135 (30 m); a few small growlers float near it (x about 1420 to 1500). Far away on the horizon at the left, the headland and the white lighthouse stand tiny (x 140 to 420, the headland up to y 282, the lighthouse a white stroke with a red cap at x 300, top y 270), and nearer, the small fishing boat sits on the water at x 560 to 620 (wheelhouse top y 286), clear of the lighthouse. Below the waterline the keel spreads wider than the top: about 130 m across (x 790 to 1505) just under the surface, widest at about 150 m (x 760 to 1585) from 25 to 60 m down (y 440 to 630), then narrowing in rounded, irregular steps to a blunt keel at about x 1130, y 960 (120 m down). The focal point is the waterline where the small top meets the huge keel. Free zones: (1) the sky above the waterline from x 120 to 820, y 40 to 250, open and calm for a narrator, a mascot or a title; (2) the deep water left of the keel from x 120 to 700, y 380 to 900, calm and clear for labels and arrows; neither is crossed by the berg. The right edge beyond x 1660 is open water and sky.
Light: The sun is about 40 degrees high at the upper right, off to the side, so the berg's top is lit cream-white on its right and top faces and pale blue in shade on its left. Under the water, light fades with depth: the water is clear blue-green just under the surface, deepening steadily to a deep navy blue at the bottom of the frame; a few soft light shafts slant down from the surface toward the lower left (lm-atmos, faint, fading by y 650). The keel glows pale turquoise near the surface and darkens to a deep blue-grey toward its bottom, with its lit side on the right. The sky is clear, pale at the horizon and deeper blue at the top.
Far layer: The sky, the distant horizon with the headland, the lighthouse and the fishing boat, the sea's surface band, and the whole underwater field with its depth gradient and light shafts.
Mid layer: The iceberg as one group with two sub-groups: berg_above (everything over the waterline) and berg_below (the keel), meeting exactly on the waterline; the growlers.
Near layer: Nothing in front: both free zones stay open.

ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- any perspective or wrong angle
- mixed grid sizes
- black outlines
- toy-like rounded blocks
- paper-thin walls
Not in this world:
- real towns, real lighthouses, flags, names on boats or buildings, signs with words, brands or logos
- a tropical or Mediterranean look: palm trees, sandy beaches, terracotta roofs, turquoise water
- a lighthouse with painted stripes, no gallery or a lantern without glazing bars
- icebergs inside the harbour, or an iceberg drawn as a floating white triangle with nothing under the water
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- a cartoon-clean place: every set shows that people live and work here
- objects at the wrong size: a person must fit through a door, a bollard reaches only to the knee
